Goal

This site shares projects I pursue outside work to practice designing, building, and testing software. The first version was a homepage, one page of notes per project, and a custom 404 page. It needed to read well on a phone and stay simple enough for me to learn from and change.

Decisions

Plain HTML and CSS

The site is text, links, and a layout that adapts to screen width. Plain HTML and CSS cover that without a build step, framework, database, or browser JavaScript, so every file can be read directly. The tradeoff is that the header and footer are repeated on each page. A static site generator becomes worth considering if the number of project pages grows.

Cloudflare hosting

I had Codex compare the free plans from Cloudflare and Vercel. Either would host a static site for $0. I chose Cloudflare because the lukemedia.dev domain is already registered there, which keeps the domain and hosting in one account.

Previewing each change before it goes live

Each change goes on its own Git branch. Cloudflare builds a preview of that branch, and the change reaches lukemedia.dev only after I merge the pull request on GitHub.

Purple accents

Purple is my favorite color, so I used it for the site's accents. Codex checked the text colors against the WCAG minimum contrast ratio of 4.5:1.

One project list with status tags

I tried separate sections for ongoing and completed projects, but the split repeated each status tag and left the completed section empty. Projects now share one list, each tagged with its status.

My role first, and no screenshots in the project list

Portfolio sites often put the person's role near the top, where readers see it first, so mine sits above the headline. I left screenshots out of the project list because my first projects wouldn't all have useful images, and a list where only some entries have one looks inconsistent. Photos go on project pages instead, where they show something a reader can't otherwise see.

A public repository for the code, and a private one for my working history

I make changes and keep my working notes in a private repository, which has the more frequent updates and my personal history. A separate public repository holds a copy of the site's code, and this site links to it.

My work and AI assistance

What I did

  • Defined the site's purpose and audience.
  • Created the GitHub repository, reviewed potential layouts, and chose the color scheme.
  • Reviewed the wording in a Google Doc, left comments, and approved the first revision of the text.
  • Added the site icon, which is a drawing of my cats (thanks for the drawing, Fern!), and updated its links on all three pages.
  • Reviewed the layout drafts, chose which changes to keep, and edited the HTML myself.
  • Changed the homepage headline and adjusted the project-section spacing in the CSS.
  • Committed, pushed, and merged each change through pull requests.
  • Tested the live site and its 404 page on my phone and desktop.

How I used AI tools

  • Had Codex research hosting options.
  • Used Codex to generate the HTML, CSS, and a local preview server, then had it revise the layout from my feedback.
  • Had Codex apply my approved wording and run local checks.
  • Gave Codex the log from a failed preview build and had it find the fix.
  • Had Cursor draft an alternative version of the wording. The site's first headline came from that draft.
  • Used Cursor to build the layout drafts and copy the version I edited and approved into the site.
  • Had Codex review other portfolio sites for common practices.
  • Used Claude to review the site's wording against my writing guide and apply the edits I chose.

Each entry in the update log says who made that change, so the balance between my code and generated code shows there as it shifts. My own code changes so far are the site icon update, the HTML edits in the October 19 layout revision, and some HTML and CSS changes in the October 24 revision.
